name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,332

entries.clue: Unruly club maybe that gives outsider a chance to play (4,4)

annotation.definition: gives outsider a chance to play
annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a relative clause hanging off 'that': the thing that gives an outsider a chance to play

blocks.note: a club is one suit of playing card; 'maybe' flags the example

annotation.surface: A rowdy sports club lets an outsider into the side.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'club' a team, but it is the card suit. A wild card is an entrant let into a tournament without qualifying.
annotation.definitionFit: A wild card is a place given to a player who has not qualified, letting an outsider play.

entries.clue: Source of oil? Fancy! (4)

blocks.note: a shaft drilled into the ground that oil is pumped up from
an old exclamation of mild surprise, as in 'Fancy that!'

annotation.surface: Someone learns where oil comes from and is duly amazed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fancy!' is the exclamation, not the adjective; 'Well!' does the same job, and an oil well is the source.
annotation.definitionFit: Oil is drawn up from a well, and 'Well!' is said in surprise just as 'Fancy!' is.

entries.clue: The French politician, source of illumination (4)

annotation.surface: A French politician is hailed as a source of enlightenment.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface wants a brilliant French statesman; 'illumination' is literal light.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain paraphrase: illumination is light, and a lamp is where a room's light comes from.

entries.clue: Can new lead support item of lighting equipment? (10)

indicatorNotes.new: the letters of 'lead' are made new, rearranged into a fresh order

blocks.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment

annotation.surface: A technician asks whether a fresh cable can hold up a stage light.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'lead' as an electric cable and 'support' as a verb; 'Can' is simply the first three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A candelabra is a branched holder for candles, a piece of lighting equipment.

entries.clue: Something to eat waiter finally put on a plate (6)

indicatorNotes.put on: in a down entry, R is placed on top of A DISH

annotation.surface: A waiter serves the food at last, putting it onto a plate.
annotation.walkthrough: Everything reads as restaurant service; the waiter contributes only his last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A radish is a crisp root vegetable eaten raw.

entries.clue: Electrical units in Hampshire (4)

indicatorNotes.in: the answer sits inside the next word

annotation.surface: A note that some electrical units are found in Hampshire.
annotation.walkthrough: Hampshire is an English county on the south coast; its name holds the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Amps (amperes) are units of electric current.

entries.clue: Paul came out to make confession of guilt (3,5)

indicatorNotes.out: the letters come out of their order and are rearranged

annotation.surface: Paul stepped forward to own up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Came out' reads as stepping out or declaring oneself; 'out' alone is the rearranging instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Mea culpa is Latin for 'my fault', an admission of guilt.

entries.clue: Normal flag (8)

blocks.note: a banner carried on a pole, as by a regiment

annotation.walkthrough: Two words, two meanings; 'flag' could also be a verb (tire), but it is the banner.
annotation.definitionFit: Standard means ordinary, and a standard is also a military or royal flag.

entries.clue: Something published in Paris about a fizzy drink (8)

indicatorNotes.about: LE MONDE goes round, about, the A

blocks.note: Le Monde, the Paris daily newspaper
taken as it stands, and goes inside after the N

annotation.surface: A Paris publication runs a piece about a fizzy drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'on the subject of'; it is the containment, with Le Monde wrapped round A.
annotation.definitionFit: In Britain lemonade usually means a clear fizzy lemon drink, which is why 'fizzy' is enough.

entries.clue: A form of domestic fuel coming back? It’s a long story (4)

blocks.note: household gas, one kind of fuel

annotation.surface: Someone complains that getting the gas supply reconnected is a long story.
annotation.walkthrough: A + GAS reads AGAS, which then runs backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A saga is a long, often rambling, narrative.

entries.clue: Nanna, silly person joining artist for sung entertainment (5,5)

annotation.surface: Granny and a fool team up with a painter to put on a show.
annotation.walkthrough: The three pieces simply follow one another; 'joining' strings them together.
annotation.definitionFit: Grand opera is serious opera sung throughout, with no spoken dialogue.

entries.clue: Circulates and buys drinks for the group (4,6)

blocks.note: in a pub, one drink for everyone in the party is a 'round'

annotation.surface: A sociable type works the room at the pub and stands everyone a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The same letters split two ways: GETS AROUND (circulates) and GETS A ROUND (of drinks). The printed enumeration (4,6) follows the first reading.
annotation.definitionFit: To get around is to circulate; to get a round is to buy drinks for everyone in the party.

entries.clue: Tree home daughter gets south of West Country river (8)

indicatorNotes.south of: in a down entry, IN and D sit below TAMAR

blocks.note: the Tamar divides Devon from Cornwall in south-west England

annotation.surface: A daughter finds a house down in the south-west of England.
annotation.walkthrough: The West Country is England's south-west; the River Tamar forms the Devon–Cornwall border.
annotation.definitionFit: The tamarind is a tropical tree grown for its tangy pods.

entries.clue: Food item — rubbish served up until start of afternoon (8)

indicatorNotes.served up: in a down entry, 'up' turns ROT upside down, to TOR

annotation.surface: A grumble that the lunch was rubbish and not served until afternoon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Served up' looks like restaurant talk, but only 'up' matters: in a down clue it flips ROT to TOR.
annotation.definitionFit: A tortilla is a thin Mexican flatbread.

entries.clue: An old playboy, not English nerd (6)

annotation.surface: A one-time ladies' man turns out to be a bit of a geek.
annotation.walkthrough: An anorak is a hooded waterproof jacket, and in British slang an obsessive enthusiast, the kind who wears one while trainspotting.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang calls an obsessive hobbyist an anorak, after the jackets worn by trainspotters.

entries.clue: Person with gun runs after bird (6)

indicatorNotes.after: 'after' means following in order, so R is written following SNIPE

blocks.note: the snipe is a wading bird
r = runs, as on a cricket scoreboard

annotation.surface: A hunter chases a bird.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Runs after' reads as chasing, but 'runs' is just R. The word for the gunman itself comes from shooting snipe, a hard bird to hit.
annotation.definitionFit: A sniper is a marksman firing from cover.

entries.clue: Way holy person catches plane? (6)

indicatorNotes.catches: ST catches, holds, TREE inside it

blocks.note: a plane is a kind of tree; the '?' flags the example. It goes between S and T

annotation.surface: A saint boards an aircraft.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plane' is the aircraft in the surface but the tree in the wordplay, common in London streets.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a way is a road, as in names like Watling Way.

entries.clue: Helping after late changes or single change (10)

indicatorNotes.after: 'after' means following in order, so RATION is written following the rearranged LATE

blocks.note: a helping = a portion, a ration

annotation.surface: Someone has a helping after a late revision, or asks for one small tweak.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Change' appears twice: the first 'changes' reorders LATE, the second sits in the definition. 'Single' fits because the answer is a countable noun, one change.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: making one alteration is making a change, and 'single' just matches the singular noun.

entries.clue: Think highly of judge (4)

blocks.note: informal: to admire or value someone
the verb: to assess or grade

annotation.surface: Someone admires a judge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like a noun after 'of', but it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: In informal use, to rate someone is to think highly of them; to rate also means to assess.

entries.clue: Tilts, dropping a glass (4)

indicatorNotes.dropping: 'dropping' means letting fall, so LEANS lets its A fall out

annotation.surface: Someone tips over and drops a glass.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface drops a drinking glass; the 'a' is the letter lost from LEANS, and 'glass' is an optical lens.
annotation.definitionFit: A lens is a shaped piece of glass that bends light; spectacles are 'glasses'.

entries.clue: I had left office, finally out of work (4)

annotation.surface: Someone who had left the office is now finally unemployed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left office' reads as resigning; 'left' is only L and the office gives its last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Idle means not working, without a job.

entries.clue: Drink ale, swallowing very little before “Time!” (8)

indicatorNotes.swallowing: to swallow is to take something inside, so BEER takes V inside it
indicatorNotes.before: 'before' means earlier in order, so BE(V)ER is written ahead of AGE

blocks.note: v = very, as a small abbreviation; it goes between BE and ER
an age = a long period of time

annotation.surface: A drinker downs a last drop of ale before the barman calls time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drink' could be the instruction in the surface, but it is the definition. "Time!" is the British pub landlord's call at closing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: beverage is the formal word for any drink, hot or cold.

entries.clue: Depict result of match finishing without winner (4)

annotation.definition2: result of match finishing without winner

blocks.note: to show in a picture, with pencil or pen

blocks.clueFragment: result of match finishing without winner
blocks.note: a game ending level, a tie

annotation.walkthrough: A long second definition follows a one-word first.
annotation.definitionFit: To draw is to depict, and a draw is a game that ends level.

entries.clue: Pilots with a maiden aboard vessels (8)

blocks.note: a + m, where m = maiden, a cricket over with no runs scored; it goes after STE

annotation.surface: Ships' pilots take a young woman on board their boats.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pilots' looks like a noun but is the verb steers. In cricket a maiden is an over in which no runs are scored, abbreviated M.
annotation.definitionFit: Steamers are steamships, vessels driven by steam.
